Shown on page 12 of Volume 11, Baptisms, St. Nicholas Ukrainian Catholic Church, Winnipeg, Manitoba on October 13, 1912.

God parents were family friends Demetrius Caryk (pronounced "Sarik") and Tecla Thiendriezsha:

The Caryk's lived on the next block on Aberdeen Avenue, about 3 doors from Kruk's towards Arlington Street:

Tekla and her husband lived in Elmwood, then moved to a shanty in East Kildonan. Mary Lacho remembered when she and her sister Kay walked to their house to see them one summer after working outside the canning factory snipping beans. They were sitting outside on their porch while they talked to them, and did not invite them in.

     As a child, Mary and her sister had lots of children to play with on their street. There were the Maly's, a Polish family who lived next door to the Boyko's and came fron the same district in the Ukraine as the Sawka's. (The name was pronounced "Moly".) "Mary (Maly) lives on Stella Avenue, and there was a girl and another small boy..."
     Mary remembered that after her mother died, she used to play there, and Mrs. Maly would buy rye bread and bologna and make sandwiches for all the children.
     Other childhood friends were the Caryk's, (a godparent of Mary): "We used to eat candy at noon!... Jean lives in Garden City, and Jack lives on Magnus Avenue. They also had another boy".
     Other kids included the Kruk boys, and John Muzyk ("John was in the choir...") and John's brothers Nick and Mike who all lived next-door to the Kruk's: "they're all dead now... Their father was a little man...short, nice, quite... I remember someone asking John once, when his father was in the hospital, how his father was doing, and John said, " if a cat won't die, you have to kill it..."  What a terrible thing to say about his father..."

(Also see notes for Josephat Sawka, Anne Lemecha, Anastasia Sawka, Catherine Sawka and Samuel Lacho for related material).

Mary Sawka attended St. Nicholas School to complete Grade 5. Mary then went to Margaret Scott School for Grade 6, but the Principal did not beleive in private schools, and put both Mary and her sister Catherine back into the grades they had just completed.

Mary Lacho was forced to repeat Grade 5, and her sister Catherine was forced to repeat Grade 3.

As per recollections of June 7, 1998: Mary Lacho also remembered that Anne Derc (who lived on the north side of Aberdeen near Sinclair) also attended Margaret Scott School at that time.

After her father sold their house to the people who owned the shanty across the lane from them, the family moved into a duplex about a block and a half east of Arlington Street, and on the south side of Aberdeen Avenue.

(As per recollections of Mary Lacho, June 7, 1998) Mary remembered suffering severe earaches while living in this house. The neighbors who lived in the house to the east of them, the Leditka family, offered a cure. Mrs. Leditka told Anne (Lemecha) to get a long strip of coarse linen and brown bees' wax. She melted the wax, and dipped the linen into it. She then rolled the waxed linen onto a stick and let it harden. Mary's mother and Mrs. Leditka then placed the candle in Mary's ear and covered her up so she would not get burnt from the sparks or melting wax. When the candle was lit, Mary remembers it creating a suction and drawing the pus out of her abcessed ear. It offerwed so much releif, that Mary asked that they do it again the next day. (Mary expressed surprise to hear that people are doing ear candling today. She said it really worked for her (about 1920).

Per recolections of January 17, 1999: Mary remembered that her parents had company, (probably while living at Kruk's home), of the Boyko's , and probably the Kruks. Her father sent her to Clayman's, a Jew who used to own a grocery store where Isaac Newton School now stands, to buy a small Ckoke bottle of homebrew. Clayman lived on Boyd Avenue, and knew the family. He had a false ceiling in his basement where he hid the homebrew. Mary did not see him fill the bottle, and he may have already had some filled to sell. He wrapped the bottle in newspaper, and Mary took it home. As it was just a small bottle, it poured only about one drink for the 6 people who shared it. 
The next day, 2 detectives came to the house. Mrs. Kruk and Anne (Lemecha) Sawka couldn't speak much English, and the two men pushed passed them at the door and began to ransack the house. The began throwing things out of a trunk that Mrs. Kruk kept pressed clothes in, and when she asked them to stop, they only began to throw more items out of the trunk, probably beleiving that that was were homebrew was being hid. They left empty handed. 
When the men came home and their wives told them what had happened, they thought it might have been a Ukrainian man who they knew (neighbor) who called the police.

One December after Anne Lemecha died and Safat remarried, Mary remembered her father being very mad at her and chasing her with a butcher knife. She ran out of the house with just what she had on, and ran over to her uncle Harry Sawka's house (a suite rented from Nelly Chiz) and stayed there for a few days before her father came to get her. Mary did not know why her father was so mad at her, or if he intended to use the knife on her. Mary said she used to keep quite, but her sister Kay used to talk back to her step-mother, and Safat may have been mad at something Kay may have done said or done.

Mary attended Isaac Newton School for Grades 7, 8, 9 and 10.

From recollections of Mary Lacho to Dennis Lacho, January 14, 1998:
Mary worked at housework after completing High School to support her father's family, and to save enough money to buy books and uniforms for a nursing course.

She worked housework for a Jewish family, who did not pay well. She then managed to find work with a Ukranian lawyer's family, the Arsenich's in East Kildonan, who were expecting a child. After the child was born, she went to work for an English family, the Carmen's on Stradbrooke Street, who paid her "better" at $15 a month.

Mr. Carmen was the manager for Whitlaw's store, which sold material, linens, and other goods. The store was later bought by Jewish brothers and became Sures Brothers.

As street car fare was $4 a month and she only received $15 a month, Mary Sawka slept at home, and walked to Stradbrooke Street in the morning, and back from work in the evening (daily)  to her father's on Aberdeen Avenue. She said it was not so bad, "because after a while you got to know where the short-cuts were, including through the railway yards".

(See picture of Mary Sawka taken in August 1931).

When Safat Sawkar was out of work, Mary paid the taxes on the house for 3 years while she worked in the operating room of St. Joseph's Hospital on Salter Street, so it would not be lost for taxes (probably around 1939, 1940, and 1941).

Antonina and Safat Sawka took out money from her, and would only leave her one ticket to go to work with, forcing her to walk home from work.

     Joan Theresa Sawka remembered being proud that her sister Mary was a nurse, and because of that, they could afford to have a telephone in their house. (as per Karen Opalick, January 14, 1998).

     Mary Lacho remembered (February 5, 1998) that she used to send dresses, ribbons to match, clothes and socks to Joan from the United States when she worked in St. Louis. She said she treated her step-sisters as her own sisters, and remembered taking them to Winnipeg Beach by train. The trip would cost 50 cents return, and you could leave on the 5:30 pm train and come back at midnight. If you waited to the next day, you had to get to the train early to get a seat.
     "You could always sell your ticket at the beach train station for 50 cents, and in the summer the train ran every two hours, as no one had cars".
     Mary also remembers she read an ad in the paper for a cottage for rent at Grand Marais. She remembered taking the street car to the couple's home to pay the rent for a week, and taking her sisters to the cottage. She also remembers Ann Padoba arrived with them and her son Clifford, and promptly stated "I'm having the couch to sleep on!" (Around 1940).

Mary Sawka finally began her 3 year nurse's training course at St. Joseph's Hospital on Salter Street when she was about 21 years old.

The hospital was run by nuns out of Toronto, and lost it's out patient clinic. The hospital could then not keep up financially, and had to be subsidized by the St. Joseph's Hospital in Toronto. (This religous sect also ran several other hospitals through the country).

The training period was to only take 3 years, with 1 year being operating room experience. She was paid $3 a month for the first year, and $4 a month for her second year, but no pay was ever really realized, because the nurses were docked for broken items, or items used or lost, such as glass syringes, pads, and other items.

During her training, Mary Sawka was assigned to maternity for too long. When her 3 years were up, she did not have her required year in the operating room. The nuns said they would graduate her without the extra experience, but offered to pay her for 2 months if she would work a year to get her experience in the operating room.

Mary accepted the offer. She was later hired on in the operating room when someone left the hospital.

     Mary Sawka graduated with top marks in her class as a Certified Registered Nurse from St. Joseph's Hospital, in Winnipeg, Manitoba on January 8, 1939.
     The Lady's Guild had a bursary for the best marks, but the Guild gave it to another nurse who was not of "foreign parentage", even though the woman did not have marks higher than Mary's.
     Mary Sawka did receive an award from Dr. W.F. Abbott (of the Abbott Clinic) on August 18, 1938 for her grades in Obstretrical Nursing, and another award in 1939 from Dr. A.C. Abbott for her grades and skills in Surgical Nursing.

Mary went to work as a Registered Nurse in St. Louis, Missouri for 6 years, including during during WW II.

Mary received a Certificate in  Basic Teaching (Nursing) Techniques & Human Relations Training while in St. Louis, Missouri on February 14, 1946.

After WW II, Mary returned to Winnipeg and taught for a year at St. Joseph's Hospital. She graduated one class, but did not like how the hospital was run.  She went to worked as a Registered Nurse at Deer Lodge Veterans Hospital in Winnipeg, Manitoba.

Mary met her husband, Sam Lacho through friend of Lena Lacho.

Prior to her marrige to Sam, Mary lived with her good friend Jessie Ozahan at 389 Penningham Street in Winnipeg from the summer of 1946 to the date of her marriage, as her step-mother said there was no room at the house on Aberdeen Avenue.

Mary and Sam Lacho were married at 4:00 pm on October 24, 1946 at Blessed Virgin Mary (BVM) Church on Boyd Avenue, Winnipeg, Manitoba. They 3 boys, Leonard, who died at birth on October 25, 1948; Gerry who was born on February 2, 1950 and baptised at BVM; and Dennis, who was born on January 6, 1953 and also baptized at BVM. (The first child, Leonard,is said to have died at birth due to complications of the umbilical cord around his neck).

Mary later worked 18 years part-time as a regisrered nurse at Winnipeg General Hospital (Health Sciences Centre) until she could not justify the costs and professional fees to the hours she was receiving from the hospital. Mary decided to retire around 1970.

Saturday, February 28, 2004, 4:25 pm, per Dennis Lacho:

Entered Seven Oaks Hospital on November 20, 2003. Had trouble swallowing, and was placed on 1 mg. morphine injections instead of Tylenol 2 tablets every 6 hours at 1:00 pm. Friday, February 27, 2004. Had earlier refused morphine, and asked hospital personnel to "do not put me to sleep". 

Died shortly after being injected with an unapproved and intentional morphine overdose by Dr. Moncek in Room 421, Unit 1 of the Palliative Care Unit of Seven Oaks Hospital.

Stopped breathing, and then heartbeat stopped at 10:47 am, Saturday, February 28, 2004. Sorry mom, I did not see what they were planning to do to you. You knew what was happening, and that is why you kept trying to reach for the injection site they placed on your right side of your abdomen. You hated it there, knew what they would do to you, and even though I stayed with you the past couple of nights, I could not protect you from them. I did not see it coming, and only realized what they were up to and what they did after I arrived in front of your house later. The reason they stripped your bed completely, changed and washed and cleaned you up is very clear now. That is why the catherter was missing from the side of yor bed. You knew, but were not able to speak to me. You could only shake your head "no" when I asked if you had any pain. As you told me only a few days earlier, doing what they did is "murder" by your definition. I will ever have to live with this. I love you and miss you Mom. I am so very sorry. Please forgive me.

Died at the age of 91 years, 4 months and 19 days.

MARY LACHO

MARY LACHO, R.N. (nee SAWKA) Mary Lacho passed away at Seven Oaks Hospital on Saturday, February 28, 2004, with her family by her side. Mary was born in North Winnipeg on October 9, 1912 to Josephat and Anna (Lemecha) Sawka. She attended St. Nicholas, Margaret Scott and Isaac Newton Schools in Winnipeg, and obtained her High School Diploma and a Nursing Certificate in Teaching and Human Relations from Washington University while working in St. Louis, Missouri. Mary was a dedicated nurse her whole life, proudly graduating at the top of her class as an R.N. in 1938 from St. Josephs Hospital in Winnipeg. Mary received the Dr. W.F. Abbott Award for Obstetrical Nursing, and later the Dr. A.C. Abbott Award for Surgical Nursing in recognition of her excellence in these fields of medicine. Her nursing career led to a move to St. Louis, Missouri during the war years, where she became a Head Nurse. Mary returned after the war to teach Nursing at St. Josephs Hospital. She went on to serve patients at the Deer Lodge and Winnipeg General Hospitals, married, raised her family, and eventually retired from the Health Sciences Centre. Mary was a member of St. Nicholas Parish, and a past member of the church choir. She enjoyed her family, friends, cooking, sewing, music, gardening, travel, warm vacations, and fishing at the family cottage. Our Mom and Grandma will always be warmly remembered for her wonderful dinners, great baking, generosity, love, wisdom, and devotion to her family. Mary is survived by her husband of 57 years, Sam; and their sons, Gerald (Margaret), and Dennis (Marie Therese). Mary deeply loved, and was especially proud of her grandchildren, Christine, Sandra, Daniel and David. Dear to Mary were her nieces, Eleanor, Brenda, and Karen; and nephew Dennis. She is also survived by her step sisters, Rose and Rae, and by many members of her Lacho, Sawka and Lemecha families. Mary Lacho was predeceased by her infant son Leonard (1948) sister Anastasia (1918) mother Anna (1921) father Josephat (1977) sister Catharine (1992) step brothers and sisters, Peter (1924), Joan (1991), and John (2000) along with many dear and close friends. Divine Liturgy will be celebrated at 1:00 p.m., Wednesday, March 3 at St. Nicholas Ukrainian Catholic Church, 737 Bannerman Ave., Winnipeg. A Basilian Father will officiate. Interment will follow at Holy Family Cemetery. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made in memory of Mary Lacho to the St. Nicholas Church Maintenance Fund, the Canadian Diabetes Association, or to a charity of ones choice. CROPO FUNERAL CHAPEL 586-8044 

As published in the Winnipeg Free Press on March 02, 2004

SAM LACHO After a brief illness and with family at his side, Sam Lacho passed away at the Pinawa Hospital on November 5, 2012 at the age of 96 years. Sam was born on November 2, 1916 to Peter and Mary (Zimak) Lechow on the family homestead near Hamrlik, a small community in the RM of Bifrost; west of Arborg, MB. He was the second of eight children. Sam attended New Valley School to Grade 8 and left home at the age of 13, finding work as a waterboy during the construction of the Seven Sisters Dam. He then joined his cousin Marion Folta and worked several years in bush camps for Sigurdsons Lumber, cutting pulp and floating log booms on the Winnipeg River. In 1937 Sam also studied Diesel Mechanics. In 1942, Sam enlisted in the army at Arborg, MB and served as a tank driver with the Ontario Regiment. Sam entered the war as a Trooper in North Africa, spending three years in the front lines of Sicily and Italy and as a senior tank crew member in Belgium and the liberation of Holland. In 1946, Sam met and married Mary Sawka, a nurse working at Deer Lodge Veterans Hospital. They settled on Cathedral Avenue in North Winnipeg to raise their family. Neighbors became good friends. In 1957, Sam obtained a cottage lot in the Lac du Bonnet area that he had been so familiar to him. In those post war years, it was at their cabin that Sam and Mary enjoyed the basics of life and countless hours of peace and tranquility while fishing, tending their rock gardens and in regular visits with their neighbors. Later in life, Sam and Mary began making annual trips to the beaches of Hawaii and Cuba. Sam worked as a Steel Fitter with Vulcan Iron Works, Bridge and Tank Western, Manitoba Bridge, and retired from Dominion Bridge in 1977. After the death of his wife Mary in 2004, Sam moved to Bona Vista Lodge in Lac du Bonnet, Manitoba. In 2006, as the years of hard work started to show their toll, Sam moved into the Lac du Bonnet Personal Care Home. Sam was a master of ingenuity and improvising and could thrive with a minimal of resources. Items people would make out of wood, Sam would design and build out of steel. Despite the odds, Sam never approached any task or situation as being impossible to accomplish. He truly enjoyed life itself and even in his last days would greet people with his familiar smile. The last few weeks and hours of Sam's life were not always kind to him. Even so, Sam never gave up hope or the fight. Sam was predeceased by his wife Mary, infant son Leonard; infant brother Peter, brothers Mike, John and Nick and sister Lena Ribachuk. Sam Lacho is survived by his son Gerry (Margaret) and granddaughters Christine and Sandra; son Dennis (Marie Therese) and grandsons Daniel and David. Also surviving are sister Anne Pongoski, brother Andy (Adele) Lacko and sister-in-law Pearl Lacko. A special thanks is expressed for past care that Sam received from the dedicated Dr. Richard Ven Gend. Special thanks are also expressed to caring staff of the Lac du Bonnet Personal Care Home, where Sam resided for the past six years. Appreciation and thanks are also expressed to friends Tony and Ali Eason, the Lac du Bonnet Legion, and the Notre Dame du Lac Roman Catholic Church for their care and visits over the years. All will miss Sam's gleaming blue eyes and smile of gratitude. Funeral Service will be held at 2:00 p.m. on Friday, November 9, 2012 at Cropo Funeral Chapel, 1442 Main Street, Winnipeg, MB. Father Isidore Dziadyk, OSBM will officiate. Interment to follow in Holy Family Cemetery. Flowers are gratefully declined. If so desired, a donation may be made to a charity of one's choice, or to the Saint Nicholas Church Building Fund. Rest in peace Dad and Grandpa - you deserve it for a job well done. God parents were family friends Demetrius Caryk (pronounced "Sarik") and Tecla Thiendriezsha:

The Caryk's lived on the next block on Aberdeen Avenue, about 3 doors from Kruk's towards Arlington Street:

Tekla and her husband lived in Elmwood, then moved to a shanty in East Kildonan. Mary Lacho remembered when she and her sister Kay walked to their house to see them one summer after working outside the canning factory snipping beans. They were sitting outside on their porch while they talked to them, and did not invite them in.

     As a child, Mary and her sister had lots of children to play with on their street. There were the Maly's, a Polish family who lived next door to the Boyko's and came fron the same district in the Ukraine as the Sawka's. (The name was pronounced "Moly".) "Mary (Maly) lives on Stella Avenue, and there was a girl and another small boy..."
     Mary remembered that after her mother died, she used to play there, and Mrs. Maly would buy rye bread and bologna and make sandwiches for all the children.
     Other childhood friends were the Caryk's, (a godparent of Mary): "We used to eat candy at noon!... Jean lives in Garden City, and Jack lives on Magnus Avenue. They also had another boy".
     Other kids included the Kruk boys, and John Muzyk ("John was in the choir...") and John's brothers Nick and Mike who all lived next-door to the Kruk's: "they're all dead now... Their father was a little man...short, nice, quite... I remember someone asking John once, when his father was in the hospital, how his father was doing, and John said, " if a cat won't die, you have to kill it..."  What a terrible thing to say about his father..."

(Also see notes for Josephat Sawka, Anne Lemecha, Anastasia Sawka, Catherine Sawka and Samuel Lacho for related material).

Mary Sawka attended St. Nicholas School to complete Grade 5. Mary then went to Margaret Scott School for Grade 6, but the Principal did not beleive in private schools, and put both Mary and her sister Catherine back into the grades they had just completed.

Mary Lacho was forced to repeat Grade 5, and her sister Catherine was forced to repeat Grade 3.

As per recollections of June 7, 1998: Mary Lacho also remembered that Anne Derc (who lived on the north side of Aberdeen near Sinclair) also attended Margaret Scott School at that time.

After her father sold their house to the people who owned the shanty across the lane from them, the family moved into a duplex about a block and a half east of Arlington Street, and on the south side of Aberdeen Avenue.

(As per recollections of Mary Lacho, June 7, 1998) Mary remembered suffering severe earaches while living in this house. The neighbors who lived in the house to the east of them, the Leditka family, offered a cure. Mrs. Leditka told Anne (Lemecha) to get a long strip of coarse linen and brown bees' wax. She melted the wax, and dipped the linen into it. She then rolled the waxed linen onto a stick and let it harden. Mary's mother and Mrs. Leditka then placed the candle in Mary's ear and covered her up so she would not get burnt from the sparks or melting wax. When the candle was lit, Mary remembers it creating a suction and drawing the pus out of her abcessed ear. It offerwed so much releif, that Mary asked that they do it again the next day. (Mary expressed surprise to hear that people are doing ear candling today. She said it really worked for her (about 1920).

Per recolections of January 17, 1999: Mary remembered that her parents had company, (probably while living at Kruk's home), of the Boyko's , and probably the Kruks. Her father sent her to Clayman's, a Jew who used to own a grocery store where Isaac Newton School now stands, to buy a small Ckoke bottle of homebrew. Clayman lived on Boyd Avenue, and knew the family. He had a false ceiling in his basement where he hid the homebrew. Mary did not see him fill the bottle, and he may have already had some filled to sell. He wrapped the bottle in newspaper, and Mary took it home. As it was just a small bottle, it poured only about one drink for the 6 people who shared it. 
The next day, 2 detectives came to the house. Mrs. Kruk and Anne (Lemecha) Sawka couldn't speak much English, and the two men pushed passed them at the door and began to ransack the house. The began throwing things out of a trunk that Mrs. Kruk kept pressed clothes in, and when she asked them to stop, they only began to throw more items out of the trunk, probably beleiving that that was were homebrew was being hid. They left empty handed. 
When the men came home and their wives told them what had happened, they thought it might have been a Ukrainian man who they knew (neighbor) who called the police.

One December after Anne Lemecha died and Safat remarried, Mary remembered her father being very mad at her and chasing her with a butcher knife. She ran out of the house with just what she had on, and ran over to her uncle Harry Sawka's house (a suite rented from Nelly Chiz) and stayed there for a few days before her father came to get her. Mary did not know why her father was so mad at her, or if he intended to use the knife on her. Mary said she used to keep quite, but her sister Kay used to talk back to her step-mother, and Safat may have been mad at something Kay may have done said or done.

Mary attended Isaac Newton School for Grades 7, 8, 9 and 10.

From recollections of Mary Lacho to Dennis Lacho, January 14, 1998:
Mary worked at housework after completing High School to support her father's family, and to save enough money to buy books and uniforms for a nursing course.

She worked housework for a Jewish family, who did not pay well. She then managed to find work with a Ukranian lawyer's family, the Arsenich's in East Kildonan, who were expecting a child. After the child was born, she went to work for an English family, the Carmen's on Stradbrooke Street, who paid her "better" at $15 a month.

Mr. Carmen was the manager for Whitlaw's store, which sold material, linens, and other goods. The store was later bought by Jewish brothers and became Sures Brothers.

As street car fare was $4 a month and she only received $15 a month, Mary Sawka slept at home, and walked to Stradbrooke Street in the morning, and back from work in the evening (daily)  to her father's on Aberdeen Avenue. She said it was not so bad, "because after a while you got to know where the short-cuts were, including through the railway yards".

(See picture of Mary Sawka taken in August 1931).

When Safat Sawkar was out of work, Mary paid the taxes on the house for 3 years while she worked in the operating room of St. Joseph's Hospital on Salter Street, so it would not be lost for taxes (probably around 1939, 1940, and 1941).

Antonina and Safat Sawka took out money from her, and would only leave her one ticket to go to work with, forcing her to walk home from work.

     Joan Theresa Sawka remembered being proud that her sister Mary was a nurse, and because of that, they could afford to have a telephone in their house. (as per Karen Opalick, January 14, 1998).

     Mary Lacho remembered (February 5, 1998) that she used to send dresses, ribbons to match, clothes and socks to Joan from the United States when she worked in St. Louis. She said she treated her step-sisters as her own sisters, and remembered taking them to Winnipeg Beach by train. The trip would cost 50 cents return, and you could leave on the 5:30 pm train and come back at midnight. If you waited to the next day, you had to get to the train early to get a seat.
     "You could always sell your ticket at the beach train station for 50 cents, and in the summer the train ran every two hours, as no one had cars".
     Mary also remembers she read an ad in the paper for a cottage for rent at Grand Marais. She remembered taking the street car to the couple's home to pay the rent for a week, and taking her sisters to the cottage. She also remembers Ann Padoba arrived with them and her son Clifford, and promptly stated "I'm having the couch to sleep on!" (Around 1940).

Mary Sawka finally began her 3 year nurse's training course at St. Joseph's Hospital on Salter Street when she was about 21 years old.

The hospital was run by nuns out of Toronto, and lost it's out patient clinic. The hospital could then not keep up financially, and had to be subsidized by the St. Joseph's Hospital in Toronto. (This religous sect also ran several other hospitals through the country).

The training period was to only take 3 years, with 1 year being operating room experience. She was paid $3 a month for the first year, and $4 a month for her second year, but no pay was ever really realized, because the nurses were docked for broken items, or items used or lost, such as glass syringes, pads, and other items.

During her training, Mary Sawka was assigned to maternity for too long. When her 3 years were up, she did not have her required year in the operating room. The nuns said they would graduate her without the extra experience, but offered to pay her for 2 months if she would work a year to get her experience in the operating room.

Mary accepted the offer. She was later hired on in the operating room when someone left the hospital.

     Mary Sawka graduated with top marks in her class as a Certified Registered Nurse from St. Joseph's Hospital, in Winnipeg, Manitoba on January 8, 1939.
     The Lady's Guild had a bursary for the best marks, but the Guild gave it to another nurse who was not of "foreign parentage", even though the woman did not have marks higher than Mary's.
     Mary Sawka did receive an award from Dr. W.F. Abbott (of the Abbott Clinic) on August 18, 1938 for her grades in Obstretrical Nursing, and another award in 1939 from Dr. A.C. Abbott for her grades and skills in Surgical Nursing.

Mary went to work as a Registered Nurse in St. Louis, Missouri for 6 years, including during during WW II.

Mary received a Certificate in  Basic Teaching (Nursing) Techniques & Human Relations Training while in St. Louis, Missouri on February 14, 1946.

After WW II, Mary returned to Winnipeg and taught for a year at St. Joseph's Hospital. She graduated one class, but did not like how the hospital was run.  She went to worked as a Registered Nurse at Deer Lodge Veterans Hospital in Winnipeg, Manitoba.

Mary met her husband, Sam Lacho through friend of Lena Lacho.

Prior to her marrige to Sam, Mary lived with her good friend Jessie Ozahan at 389 Penningham Street in Winnipeg from the summer of 1946 to the date of her marriage, as her step-mother said there was no room at the house on Aberdeen Avenue.

Mary and Sam Lacho were married at 4:00 pm on October 24, 1946 at Blessed Virgin Mary (BVM) Church on Boyd Avenue, Winnipeg, Manitoba. They 3 boys, Leonard, who died at birth on October 25, 1948; Gerry who was born on February 2, 1950 and baptised at BVM; and Dennis, who was born on January 6, 1953 and also baptized at BVM. (The first child, Leonard,is said to have died at birth due to complications of the umbilical cord around his neck).

Mary later worked 18 years part-time as a regisrered nurse at Winnipeg General Hospital (Health Sciences Centre) until she could not justify the costs and professional fees to the hours she was receiving from the hospital. Mary decided to retire around 1970.

Saturday, February 28, 2004, 4:25 pm, per Dennis Lacho:

Entered Seven Oaks Hospital on November 20, 2003. Had trouble swallowing, and was placed on 1 mg. morphine injections instead of Tylenol 2 tablets every 6 hours at 1:00 pm. Friday, February 27, 2004. Had earlier refused morphine, and asked hospital personnel to "do not put me to sleep". 

Died shortly after being injected with an unapproved and intentional morphine overdose by Dr. Moncek in Room 421, Unit 1 of the Palliative Care Unit of Seven Oaks Hospital.

Stopped breathing, and then heartbeat stopped at 10:47 am, Saturday, February 28, 2004. Sorry mom, I did not see what they were planning to do to you. You knew what was happening, and that is why you kept trying to reach for the injection site they placed on your right side of your abdomen. You hated it there, knew what they would do to you, and even though I stayed with you the past couple of nights, I could not protect you from them. I did not see it coming, and only realized what they were up to and what they did after I arrived in front of your house later. The reason they stripped your bed completely, changed and washed and cleaned you up is very clear now. That is why the catherter was missing from the side of yor bed. You knew, but were not able to speak to me. You could only shake your head "no" when I asked if you had any pain. As you told me only a few days earlier, doing what they did is "murder" by your definition. I will ever have to live with this. I love you and miss you Mom. I am so very sorry. Please forgive me.

Died at the age of 91 years, 4 months and 19 days.

MARY LACHO

MARY LACHO, R.N. (nee SAWKA) Mary Lacho passed away at Seven Oaks Hospital on Saturday, February 28, 2004, with her family by her side. Mary was born in North Winnipeg on October 9, 1912 to Josephat and Anna (Lemecha) Sawka. She attended St. Nicholas, Margaret Scott and Isaac Newton Schools in Winnipeg, and obtained her High School Diploma and a Nursing Certificate in Teaching and Human Relations from Washington University while working in St. Louis, Missouri. Mary was a dedicated nurse her whole life, proudly graduating at the top of her class as an R.N. in 1938 from St. Josephs Hospital in Winnipeg. Mary received the Dr. W.F. Abbott Award for Obstetrical Nursing, and later the Dr. A.C. Abbott Award for Surgical Nursing in recognition of her excellence in these fields of medicine. Her nursing career led to a move to St. Louis, Missouri during the war years, where she became a Head Nurse. Mary returned after the war to teach Nursing at St. Josephs Hospital. She went on to serve patients at the Deer Lodge and Winnipeg General Hospitals, married, raised her family, and eventually retired from the Health Sciences Centre. Mary was a member of St. Nicholas Parish, and a past member of the church choir. She enjoyed her family, friends, cooking, sewing, music, gardening, travel, warm vacations, and fishing at the family cottage. Our Mom and Grandma will always be warmly remembered for her wonderful dinners, great baking, generosity, love, wisdom, and devotion to her family. Mary is survived by her husband of 57 years, Sam; and their sons, Gerald (Margaret), and Dennis (Marie Therese). Mary deeply loved, and was especially proud of her grandchildren, Christine, Sandra, Daniel and David. Dear to Mary were her nieces, Eleanor, Brenda, and Karen; and nephew Dennis. She is also survived by her step sisters, Rose and Rae, and by many members of her Lacho, Sawka and Lemecha families. Mary Lacho was predeceased by her infant son Leonard (1948) sister Anastasia (1918) mother Anna (1921) father Josephat (1977) sister Catharine (1992) step brothers and sisters, Peter (1924), Joan (1991), and John (2000) along with many dear and close friends. Divine Liturgy will be celebrated at 1:00 p.m., Wednesday, March 3 at St. Nicholas Ukrainian Catholic Church, 737 Bannerman Ave., Winnipeg. A Basilian Father will officiate. Interment will follow at Holy Family Cemetery. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made in memory of Mary Lacho to the St. Nicholas Church Maintenance Fund, the Canadian Diabetes Association, or to a charity of ones choice. CROPO FUNERAL CHAPEL 586-8044

MARY LACHO, R.N. (nee SAWKA) Mary Lacho passed away at Seven Oaks Hospital on Saturday, February 28, 2004, with her family by her side. Mary was born in North Winnipeg on October 9, 1912 to Josephat and Anna (Lemecha) Sawka. She attended St. Nicholas, Margaret Scott and Isaac Newton Schools in Winnipeg, and obtained her High School Diploma and a Nursing Certificate in Teaching and Human Relations from Washington University while working in St. Louis, Missouri. Mary was a dedicated nurse her whole life, proudly graduating at the top of her class as an R.N. in 1938 from St. Josephs Hospital in Winnipeg. Mary received the Dr. W.F. Abbott Award for Obstetrical Nursing, and later the Dr. A.C. Abbott Award for Surgical Nursing in recognition of her excellence in these fields of medicine. Her nursing career led to a move to St. Louis, Missouri during the war years, where she became a Head Nurse. Mary returned after the war to teach Nursing at St. Josephs Hospital. She went on to serve patients at the Deer Lodge and Winnipeg General Hospitals, married, raised her family, and eventually retired from the Health Sciences Centre. Mary was a member of St. Nicholas Parish, and a past member of the church choir. She enjoyed her family, friends, cooking, sewing, music, gardening, travel, warm vacations, and fishing at the family cottage. Our Mom and Grandma will always be warmly remembered for her wonderful dinners, great baking, generosity, love, wisdom, and devotion to her family. Mary is survived by her husband of 57 years, Sam; and their sons, Gerald (Margaret), and Dennis (Marie Therese). Mary deeply loved, and was especially proud of her grandchildren, Christine, Sandra, Daniel and David. Dear to Mary were her nieces, Eleanor, Brenda, and Karen; and nephew Dennis. She is also survived by her step sisters, Rose and Rae, and by many members of her Lacho, Sawka and Lemecha families. Mary Lacho was predeceased by her infant son Leonard (1948) sister Anastasia (1918) mother Anna (1921) father Josephat (1977) sister Catharine (1992) step brothers and sisters, Peter (1924), Joan (1991), and John (2000) along with many dear and close friends. Divine Liturgy will be celebrated at 1:00 p.m., Wednesday, March 3 at St. Nicholas Ukrainian Catholic Church, 737 Bannerman Ave., Winnipeg. A Basilian Father will officiate. Interment will follow at Holy Family Cemetery. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made in memory of Mary Lacho to the St. Nicholas Church Maintenance Fund, the Canadian Diabetes Association, or to a charity of ones choice.
